match.reason: No point in the bank covers how staff leave a business; the closest, on why businesses close, is about the business ending rather than employees separating from it.

draft.title: Separation
card: Separation is when an employee leaves a business. It is the last stage of the human resource process.
Resignation
the employee chooses to leave. They give notice, as set by their award or contract.
Redundancy
the employer no longer needs the job done, for example after new technology or a restructure. The worker has not done anything wrong.
Dismissal
the employer ends the job because of the employee's conduct or performance. It must be fair under the Fair Work Act, with a valid reason and a fair process.
draft.remember: Separation is any way a worker leaves. Who decides, and why, sets the type.

a.q: Kyle's employer closes a warehouse because machines now do the work. Kyle's job no longer exists. Which type of separation is this?
opts: Redundancy
Dismissal
Resignation
Retirement
a.why: The employer no longer needs the job done, and Kyle has done nothing wrong, so it is redundancy. Dismissal is the tempting option, but it relates to the employee's conduct or performance, not to the job disappearing.
a.clue: Ask whether the job is gone or the worker is the problem.

b.q: Priya's manager ends her job after repeated warnings about missing safety checks. Why must the business follow a fair process?
opts: Dismissal must be fair, with a valid reason and process
Dismissal is a choice, so the worker must agree to it
Redundancy rules apply, as the employer decided to end it
Notice is only needed when an employee resigns
b.why: This is dismissal, because the employer ended the job over Priya's conduct. The Fair Work Act expects a valid reason and a fair process. It is not redundancy, as the job still exists and the reason is her conduct.
b.clue: The employer ended the job because of what the worker did.

b.best: Dismissal must be fair, with a valid reason and process

proposal.title: Separation
card: Resignation
the employee chooses to leave, often for another job. They give notice, as set by their award or contract.
Retirement
the employee chooses to leave the workforce, usually late in their career. An employer generally cannot force a worker to retire because of their age.
Redundancy
the employer no longer needs the job done, for example after new technology or a restructure. The worker has not done anything wrong.
Dismissal
the employer ends the job because of the employee's conduct or performance. Under the Fair Work Act, it needs a valid reason and a fair process.
proposal.remember: Separation is any way a worker leaves. Who decides, and why, sets the type.

a.q: Kyle's employer closes a warehouse because machines now do the work. Kyle's job no longer exists. Which type of separation is this?
opts: Redundancy
Dismissal
Resignation
Retirement
a.why: The employer no longer needs the job done, and Kyle has done nothing wrong, so it is redundancy. Dismissal is the tempting option, but it relates to the employee's conduct or performance, not to the job disappearing.
a.clue: Ask whether the job is gone or the worker is the problem.

b.q: Priya's manager ends her job after repeated warnings about missing safety checks. What does the Fair Work Act expect the business to have?
opts: A valid reason and a proper process for ending it
Proof that her job is no longer needed by anyone
Priya's written agreement that she will leave
Notice from Priya, as set by her award or contract
b.why: This is dismissal, because the employer ended the job over Priya's conduct, so the Fair Work Act expects a valid reason and a fair process. Showing the job is no longer needed fits redundancy, but Priya's job still exists and the reason is her conduct.
b.clue: Was the job ended because of the job itself or the worker?

b.best: A valid reason and a proper process for ending it
